checklist.title: A podcast clip worth sharing starts with a complete thought.
checklist.metadataTitle: Podcast Clip Checklist: What to Check Before Publishing
checklist.description: A practical podcast clip checklist: review context, the cut, captions, framing, and the final file before you publish. Includes a printable review sheet.
checklist.intro: Use this checklist to decide what to keep, what to fix, and what to leave out. It works whether your first cut comes from AI or from you.

sections.title: 01 / Start with the listener test
sections.body:
Play the candidate without watching the preceding conversation. Can someone who has never heard your podcast explain who or what the speaker is talking about, and what point they are making? If not, the clip needs more context before it needs a stronger headline.

Listen for openings such as ‘that’s why,’ ‘he did it,’ or ‘the second thing.’ They can work when the subject is already clear, but often signal that the real beginning sits a few sentences earlier. Add only the setup that the thought needs, then watch again from the new starting point.
checks: The subject is clear without the previous conversation.
The first sentence gives the listener a reason to keep watching.

example.before: That’s why I stopped doing it.
example.after: I used to rewrite every interview question during the recording. That’s why I stopped doing it.
example.explanation: Illustrative writing example, not a product result. The second version identifies the habit. In a real clip, recover the speaker’s actual setup from the source; do not invent a sentence or make them say something new.

sections.title: 02 / Keep the answer, not just the question
sections.body:
A provocative question can be a good opening, but it is not automatically a complete clip. Keep the answer, example, or conclusion that makes the moment useful on its own. If you are intentionally making a teaser, make that promise clear instead of presenting it as a complete explanation.

Check both boundaries by listening to the original audio. A cut can fall between transcript words and still interrupt a breath, qualification, or conclusion. Extend it when needed. If no clean, self-contained cut is available, choose another moment.
checks: The answer or payoff is present.
The start and end sound natural when played aloud.

sections.title: 03 / Check what the cut leaves out
sections.body:
Read or listen to the surrounding conversation before approving a candidate. A speaker might be quoting someone, describing a mistake, or making a point that they qualify in the next sentence. A shorter clip should still represent what they meant.

Review the proposed headline separately. A title that sounds compelling but changes the topic is a reason to rewrite the title. Also identify sponsor reads and calls to buy a product; do not mistake a polished advertisement for an editorial highlight.
checks: The cut preserves the speaker’s meaning and any essential qualification.
The title describes this clip accurately.
Sponsor content is identified and selected intentionally.

sections.title: 04 / Give each clip a different job
sections.body:
Compare the clips you plan to keep. Three cuts of the same answer may add less variety than a useful explanation, a personal story, and a thoughtful disagreement. Choose based on what each clip contributes, not how many candidates the tool produced.

Write one sentence describing why you would share each candidate. If you cannot name its value without a generic phrase such as ‘interesting moment,’ revisit the selection. Keep fewer clips when that produces a clearer, more useful set.
checks: This clip adds a distinct idea, story, or perspective to the set.
I can explain why my audience would find it useful.

sections.title: 05 / Watch the whole vertical frame
sections.body:
Play the entire clip, including camera cuts, gestures, and changes of speaker. A crop that works at the start may hide someone later. Check both people in a conversation, and look for slides or objects that the speaker refers to.

If a tight portrait crop loses essential information, use a wider composition or fit the complete source frame where your editor supports it. A visible face is not enough if the example being discussed has disappeared. Preview the video in the destination app before posting, because interface overlays can cover the image.
checks: People and essential visual information remain visible throughout.
Captions and titles do not cover faces or important details.

sections.title: 06 / Read every caption against the audio
sections.body:
Check names, numbers, technical terms, and short words such as ‘not.’ These can change the meaning even when most of the transcript is correct. Listen while reading rather than relying only on spellcheck.

Review the captions at a phone-sized display. Check line breaks, contrast, and timing, especially when the speaker talks quickly. Keep the wording faithful to the source and avoid adding a headline that competes with the captions for attention.
checks: Names, numbers, negations, and specialist terms match the audio.
Captions remain readable and follow the speech.

sections.title: 07 / Review the file you will actually publish
sections.body:
Open the downloaded video and play it from beginning to end with sound. Check the first and last frames, caption timing, framing, and audio. The file you approve should be the latest version, not an earlier download from before your final edits.

Confirm that you have permission to use the recording and any added media. Check the cover and post copy against the finished cut. Save the reviewed file with a name that makes its version clear, then preview the upload in your destination app before publishing.
checks: The downloaded file plays correctly with sound from start to finish.
The cover and post copy match this final version.
I have permission to publish the recording and added media.

tutorial.title: How to clip podcasts for TikTok.
tutorial.metadataTitle: How to Clip Podcasts for TikTok
tutorial.description: Choose a complete podcast moment, refine its vertical framing and captions, and export a clip for TikTok with Scribix.
tutorial.intro: A good podcast clip gives someone who missed the full episode enough context to understand one useful idea. Start with the moment you want to share, then refine the cut, picture and captions around it. This guide covers making a vertical video from a filmed podcast or interview in Scribix and downloading the finished file. Uploading that file to TikTok is a separate step.
tutorial.walkthroughCaption: From an existing podcast project to a downloadable clip: compare candidates, review the words, inspect framing and captions, then view the actual export. The overview combines real screenshots and footage; it does not show processing time. Source: Changeover Podcast.

sections.title: Before you start
sections.body:
Use a video recording that you have permission to publish. Keep the original audio: you will need to listen to the speaker while reviewing the cut and checking the captions. An audio-only episode belongs in the transcription workflow, rather than this video-clipping workflow.

Free accounts can export AI-generated clips as-is. Adjusting clip boundaries, captions, framing and branding requires a paid plan. Check current plans before following the editing steps below.

Start with a local video file. The YouTube transcript tool imports captions; it does not import the original YouTube video into this clipping workflow.

sections.title: 1. Upload your podcast recording
sections.body:
Open Scribix and choose the video file from your device. Follow the upload and processing status shown on screen. Keep the upload page open while the file is being transferred.

For the example below, we resumed an already uploaded project. The upload instructions explain how to start your own project; a new upload is not shown in the demonstration.

Begin with one recording so that you can review the results against the original conversation. Do not judge the job by the number of clips it produces: some episodes contain more self-contained moments than others.

sections.title: 2. Choose a moment that makes sense on its own
sections.body:
Play a suggested clip before editing it. Ask three questions:

Is the subject clear to someone who has not heard the episode?

Does the clip contain an answer, explanation, story or conclusion?

Does the headline accurately describe what the speaker says?

Listen to the surrounding conversation when a candidate opens with a vague reference or a reply to an unheard question. Watch for sponsor reads and repeated versions of the same idea. Keep the candidates that offer something distinct to your audience.

The podcast clip checklist gives you a repeatable review for these decisions.
sections.imageAlt: Four podcast candidates and the selected clip in Scribix
sections.imageCaption: This 9 min 47 sec recording already had four candidates. We opened the first, covering 00:01.663–00:59.087. Its topic is the player’s composure; the other candidates discuss tactics, other players and relatability.

sections.title: 3. Refine the start and finish
sections.body:
With a paid plan, use the transcript and clip boundaries to find a natural opening. Include the question or setup if the answer depends on it. At the end, keep the sentence that completes the point rather than stopping immediately after the most dramatic phrase.

Play the new cut with sound. A boundary that looks neat in text can still interrupt a breath or remove a qualification. If you cannot recover a complete thought within a useful clip, choose a different moment.
sections.imageAlt: Content panel showing transcript and source start and end controls
sections.imageCaption: Choose Edit clip, then Content to review the transcript and original video start/end times. The source range in this example stays at 00:01.663–00:59.087.

sections.title: 4. Check the vertical picture
sections.body:
Watch the whole portrait composition, not just its first frame. Follow changes of speaker, camera cuts and gestures. Check that the crop keeps the person and anything they refer to visible.

Adjust the framing when it loses important information. A wider composition can be preferable to a close-up when two people or a presentation need to remain in view. Do not assume that automatic framing has handled every transition correctly.
sections.imageAlt: Framing controls beside the portrait podcast preview
sections.imageCaption: The Framing panel offers Automatic follow, Show full frame and Crop a section manually. Automatic follow was already selected here. This output retains black space above and below the picture; review camera changes before deciding whether to adjust it.
sections.relatedLabel: Choosing between a crop and the full frame? Read the horizontal-to-vertical framing guide

sections.title: 5. Correct and style the captions
sections.body:
Listen while reading the captions. Pay particular attention to names, numbers, specialist terms and words such as “not.” Correct the text before choosing the style.

Review the result at a phone-sized display. Check line breaks, contrast, timing and placement. Avoid covering the speaker’s face or making an opening title compete with the captions. Check placement again in TikTok’s upload preview, where the app adds its own interface.
sections.imageAlt: Captions panel with motion style, colors, size and position controls
sections.imageCaption: This example uses Karaoke punch, white text and a yellow highlight. Open Correct transcript text to review wording. Check the spoken names against the audio before publishing.

sections.title: 6. Export and review the actual file
sections.body:
Choose Download in the clip editor. While the render is running, the control shows Preparing your video. When the file is ready, use Download to save it. The example below was generated from this project during the walkthrough.

Generate the finished clip and download it. Play the downloaded video from beginning to end with sound. Check the cut, captions, framing, first and last frames, and audio.

Make sure your cover and post copy describe this final version. If you change the clip after exporting, create and review the updated file before publishing. Keep the approved download clearly named so that you do not upload an older draft.
sections.videoCaption: The actual 57-second portrait export, with original audio and captions. Play it to review the camera changes, wording and framing. This candidate was exported as-is; use the checks above before publishing your own clip. Source: Changeover Podcast.

sections.title: Before you post
sections.body:
Preview the file in TikTok and check how the video looks with the platform interface around it. Confirm your intended audience and post details there. This walkthrough does not assume that your Scribix account is connected to TikTok or that a direct publishing flow has been tested.

You do not need to publish every suggested clip. A smaller set of clear, accurate moments can serve your audience better than a batch you have not reviewed.

Start with your video podcast.

reframing.title: How to turn horizontal video vertical without cutting off speakers
reframing.metadataTitle: Horizontal video to vertical: keep speakers in frame
reframing.description: Choose between cropping and keeping the full frame. Learn how to reframe one speaker, a two-person interview or a screen recording for a 9:16 clip.
reframing.intro: A horizontal recording does not become a useful vertical clip just because you change its shape. Decide what the viewer needs to see, then choose a crop or keep the whole frame. Here is how to make that decision before you export.

sections.title: 01 / Without cropping, or without losing the speaker?
sections.body:
These are different goals. To keep every part of a landscape frame inside a portrait canvas, scale the full image down. A wide recording will leave space above and below. To fill that same canvas, crop away some of the sides and choose which part remains visible.

A 16:9 picture cannot fill a 9:16 frame while preserving its proportions and every original edge. Stretching distorts people; rotating makes them sideways. Neither solves the framing problem. Start with the full frame when both sides contain essential information, and crop only when a narrower view still tells the story.

diagram.title: One scene, three framing choices

items.title: Fixed centre crop
items.body: The middle can miss both speakers.

items.title: Crop toward a speaker
items.body: One person is visible; the other is outside the frame.

items.title: Keep the full frame
items.body: Both stay visible, with empty space above and below.

diagram.caption: Illustration of framing geometry, not a Scribix export or an automatic tracking test.

sections.title: 02 / One speaker: check the movement, not just the first frame
sections.body:
For a talking-head clip, begin with a crop around the person who is speaking. Leave room above the head and around any hand gesture or object that explains the point. Play the whole passage: a crop that works at the start may fail when the speaker leans sideways.

Automatic following is a starting point to review. If it loses the subject, adjust the framing over the affected section rather than trusting a still preview. Use a wider composition or keep the full image when the movement will not fit. Zooming in cannot recover detail missing from the source.

sections.title: 03 / Two people: decide whether the reaction matters
sections.body:
In a wide interview, a fixed centre crop may show the space between the guests. Following the current speaker can work for a self-contained answer, but it hides the other person’s reaction. If that reaction changes the meaning, keep both people visible.

Use the full-frame option when the conversation needs both sides. You will trade larger faces for more context. Scribix does not currently offer a two-person split-screen layout; do not plan a stacked composition around that feature. Check every change of speaker and moments when both speak at once.

sections.title: 04 / A screen recording needs a different decision
sections.body:
A face is not always the subject. For software demos and slide presentations, identify the button, chart or text the viewer must read. A crop that follows the presenter can remove the actual explanation.

Keeping the full frame preserves information, but small interface text may become unreadable on a phone. Pick a shorter passage about one screen area and frame that area if possible. If the task requires the whole desktop and a separate face view, use an editor that supports that layout; Scribix does not currently provide a presenter-plus-screen split view.

sections.title: 05 / Apply the choice in Scribix
sections.body:
Upload an original video file you have permission to use, then choose a suggested clip or select a passage yourself on a paid plan. This workflow produces short portrait clips; it is not a converter for exporting an entire recording at any aspect ratio. YouTube transcript import does not import the original video for clipping.

Open the editor’s framing controls. Review Auto for the suggested framing, use Fit to retain the full source picture, or adjust the crop and zoom for the part you want to show. For changes during the clip, work with the framing sections, preview the transitions and save your adjustments before exporting.

Framing adjustments and caption editing require a paid plan. Free accounts can review and export the original AI candidates. After choosing the frame, correct captions and check their position so that they do not cover the face or important screen content.
sections.imageAlt: Existing Scribix framing panel showing a portrait preview and framing controls
sections.imageCaption: Existing Framing screenshot from our podcast guide. Source: Changeover Podcast. This is interface evidence, not a new crop comparison; the screenshot and source subtitles retain their original language.

sections.title: 06 / Check the exported file on a phone
sections.body:
Watch the saved MP4 with sound, from beginning to end. If a head disappears, inspect the corresponding framing section. If there are black bars, check whether you deliberately kept the whole image or whether the bars are already part of the uploaded file. Cropping them away may also remove useful content.

If the result looks soft, reduce the zoom and return to the best original file available. Re-exporting at a larger size does not recreate detail lost in a tight crop. Check the video in the destination app’s preview as well: interface overlays can cover captions even when they fit inside your exported frame.

The example below is an existing portrait export with its original letterboxing. It shows that a 9:16 file can retain a wide picture. It is not evidence that Fit was selected or that automatic framing improved this shot.
sections.videoCaption: Existing 57-second Scribix export from the podcast guide, with original audio, captions and letterboxing. Source: Changeover Podcast. No new before-and-after test was performed.
checks: The important person or detail stays visible throughout.
Speaker changes and framing transitions are comfortable to watch.
Captions remain readable without hiding essential content.
I checked the exported file and the destination app preview.

podcast.editTitle: The details are part of the story.

faqs.question: Can I try the podcast clip maker for free?
faqs.answer: Free includes {minutes} minutes of uploaded media processing as a one-time allowance. You can export AI-generated clips as-is. Editing and brand controls require a paid plan.

faqs.question: Do I need a video podcast?
faqs.answer: Start with a filmed podcast, interview or conversation. For audio-only episodes, use audio to text to work with the transcript; that is a separate workflow.

faqs.question: Can I paste a YouTube link to make clips?
faqs.answer: This clipping workflow starts with a local video file. The YouTube transcript tool imports captions, not the original video for clipping.

faqs.question: Can I change the clips the AI selects?
faqs.answer: With a paid plan, adjust the boundaries, caption text and style, and framing. Review the surrounding conversation to preserve the speaker’s meaning.

faqs.question: Does Scribix guarantee a certain number of clips or views?
faqs.answer: No. Useful moments depend on the recording. Review suggestions for context and relevance; a suggested clip is not a prediction of views or engagement.
